findings.text: The first paragraph tells a newcomer what Athena is and what makes it different, in plain words. It is the only real description of Athena on the page, and it is clear.
findings.source: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. It shows how it read the request, has one AI model do the work and a different one check it, and records what each step cost."

findings.text: The page lives at Athena's address, but its title and almost all of its body are about another project, firstmate. Someone who came to learn about Athena may not be sure which of the two is the product. The page never says why they should care about firstmate in particular.

This explains why the page exists, and the study does what it promises: every statement links to a claim, and every claim links to file and line ranges at a fixed commit. That works well as a demonstration.
findings.source: "Athena made this study of firstmate to show that it can read an unfamiliar project and explain it with every statement traced to a claim, and every claim to lines in the project's own files."

findings.text: The next step is easy to find, because the header links to it. But the install steps are thin. There is no clone command, no list of prerequisites (such as a Rust toolchain, model access or API keys), and no word on what `athena ask` produces or what it might cost.
findings.source: Next steps: "Install Athena from a checkout of its repository: ./setup.sh" and "Try it with a one-line request: athena ask "add a changelog""

findings.text: The firstmate overview is well ordered: what it is, one piece of work from start to finish, then failures and missing limits. A newcomer can follow it.
findings.source: Start here / "What firstmate is": "Firstmate is a tool that keeps a backlog of programming tasks and hands each one to a separate AI coding tool, called a worker..."

findings.text: A newcomer meets a lot of firstmate-specific terms before the substance: captain, yolo, secondmate, scout, harness, stale wake. The Glossary repeats many of them. This makes the page heavy for a first visit, even though the definitions are careful.
Transitions are referred to by id before the Transitions section defines them, so a reader going top to bottom has to jump ahead.
findings.source: Counters: "places-held, changed by transitions t1, t3, t4, t9, t11"

findings.text: The t4 card says cleanup frees the place, without adding that a ship with a PR already freed its place at t3. A careful reader may think the place is freed twice.
findings.source: t4 card: "Cleanup frees the place." vs t3 card: "A recorded PR frees the worker's place"

findings.text: The section promises three parts, but four subheadings follow, starting with "Words used first". This is a small mismatch.
findings.source: Start here: "The three parts below say what firstmate is, follow one piece of work, and say what happens when something fails or has no limit."

findings.text: The page is open about the fact that nothing was run, and it gives no test for what counts as "in scope" rather than guessing. This honesty helps the reader trust the page.
findings.source: Limits of this study, f1: "This study read the pinned tree only... no failure or retry edge was observed; every claim is marked read."

findings.text: This mentions a `studies/` folder without saying it is in Athena's repository. A newcomer cannot tell where to find it.
findings.source: About this page: "the name of the folder under studies/ that holds the data this page is generated from"
